newsitem.title: USA: Implantable artificial heart seen by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Implantable artificial heart seen by 2000.

text.p: A leading heart surgeon said on Monday he expected a totally implantable artificial heart to be ready for human testing by the year 2000.

Dr. O.H. "Bud" Frazier of the Texas Heart Institute said the institute and Massachusetts-based ABIOMED Inc. were developing the heart for permanent use, although its first use would likely be for patients awaiting transplants.
"Our goal is to assist heart patients in resuming normal lives ... We anticipate by the year 2000 the ABIOMED total artificial heart will be ready for clinical trials," Frazier said in a statement.
The Texas Heart Institute, based in Houston, and ABIOMED have received an $8.5 million federal grant to complete testing the of the heart, Frazier said.
ABIOMED vice president Robert Kung told the Houston Chronicle that the government contract calls for developing a heart that lasts at least five years, but the company's goal is much higher.
"We intend it to last as long as the person lives," he said.

The ABIOMED heart, which has been in development for nine years, is a grapefruit-sized, battery-powered pump capable of pushing up to 10 liters (10.6 quarts) of blood a minute through the body. At rest, the human heart pumps five to seven liters (5.3 to 7.4 quarts) a minute.
It has internal batteries, but most of the time would be powered by external batteries hooked to a transmitter coil in the skin.
The external batteries could be removed for brief periods and the heart would run on its internal power, Frazier said.
The heart also has the ability to speed up or slow down based on the body's demands.
Frazier said the next phase of research is to verify the reliability and performance of the artificial heart before starting human trials.
The Texas Heart Institute, located in St. Luke's Episcopal Hospital, was the site of the first artificial heart implant in a human in 1969.
